blindSummary:
This state/province is one of twelve in the country operating a parallel religious criminal-code system, and one of five where activity by a government-backed religious morality-police body is specifically documented in a report of an international religious-freedom monitoring commission. Religious-law courts hold criminal jurisdiction over adherents of the state religion, reaching conduct beyond the federal same-sex-marriage prohibition law — including same-sex acts between women. No trans-specific incident or carried-out capital sentence is on record here.

The enacted religious-law criminal jurisdiction combined with documented religious morality-police enforcement infrastructure places this state/province's practical risk above that of the seven religious-law states/provinces with no documented morality-police activity; a neighbouring state/province — whose 2000 adoption of the system triggered the cascade of adoptions — is placed almost identically, its distinction being that the morality-police presence here is explicitly documented.
